planting.note: Broadcast or drill in early spring or late summer into moist, fine-textured to heavy soil in full sun; narrow-leaf trefoil tolerates seasonally wet, saline, and alkaline soils better than most forage legumes.

directions: Broadcast or drill in early spring or late summer into moist, fine-textured to heavy soil in full sun; narrow-leaf trefoil tolerates seasonally wet, saline, and alkaline soils better than most forage legumes. A finer-stemmed, more prostrate relative of birdsfoot trefoil, it forms a low, spreading mat of narrow leaflets and small yellow pea-like flowers that fix nitrogen and provide non-bloating, palatable grazing for livestock without the bloat risk of clover. It persists in seasonally flooded pastures, saline lowlands, and heavy clay soils where alfalfa and clover struggle, making it a useful forage and cover legume for difficult, poorly drained ground. Once established it tolerates close, frequent grazing and self-seeds to maintain a persistent stand with minimal reseeding.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Guide

planting.note: Broadcast seed or plant sprigs after soil has warmed following last frost, into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; digitgrass is a subtropical grass that establishes and spreads quickly in hot weather.

directions: Broadcast seed or plant sprigs after soil has warmed following last frost, into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; digitgrass is a subtropical grass that establishes and spreads quickly in hot weather. A leafy, stoloniferous perennial forage grass native to Africa, it forms a dense, fast-spreading sod of soft, palatable leaves that livestock readily graze, and it recovers quickly after cutting or heavy grazing through the warm season. It tolerates moderate drought and a range of soil types better than many tropical forage grasses, and is widely used for pasture, hay, and erosion control on sloped or disturbed ground in subtropical regions. Fertilize with nitrogen after each grazing or cutting cycle to sustain the vigorous regrowth that makes it a high-yielding warm-season forage.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Guide

planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed into warm, moist, well-drained soil in full sun well after last frost; palisade grass is a tropical species that needs consistently warm soil to germinate and establishes best during the height of summer heat.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed into warm, moist, well-drained soil in full sun well after last frost; palisade grass is a tropical species that needs consistently warm soil to germinate and establishes best during the height of summer heat. This robust, tufted to shortly rhizomatous tropical forage grass produces abundant, leafy growth and deep, extensive roots that make it highly productive on acidic, low-fertility soils where many other forage grasses fail, and it is among the most widely planted pasture grasses across the tropics. It tolerates heavy grazing pressure and recovers rapidly, while its deep root system provides excellent erosion control on sloped or degraded pasture land. It is frost-sensitive and behaves as an annual outside consistently frost-free climates, going dormant or dying back with the first freeze.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Guide

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in late summer to early fall, or early spring, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; smooth brome is extremely winter hardy and best established well ahead of the first hard freeze for strong root development.

directions: Drill or broadcast in late summer to early fall, or early spring, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; smooth brome is extremely winter hardy and best established well ahead of the first hard freeze for strong root development. A long-lived, sod-forming, cool-season perennial grass with an extensive rhizome system, it produces abundant, leafy, palatable forage for hay and pasture across the northern plains and upper Midwest, tolerating both severe winter cold and summer drought once its deep root system is established. It is commonly seeded in mixtures with alfalfa or other legumes for balanced, high-yielding hay, and its dense sod makes it valuable for erosion control on waterways and roadsides. Allow a full growing season for establishment before heavy grazing or haying, and fertilize with nitrogen in years without a legume companion to sustain yield.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Guide

planting.note: Seed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option, into finely prepared, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade; creeping bentgrass requires intensive mowing, watering, and fertility management to perform well and is not a low-maintenance lawn choice.

directions: Seed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option, into finely prepared, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade; creeping bentgrass requires intensive mowing, watering, and fertility management to perform well and is not a low-maintenance lawn choice. This fine-textured, stoloniferous cool-season grass spreads by surface runners to form an extremely dense, smooth, uniform turf when mowed very short, making it the standard grass for golf greens, tees, and fairways in cool and transition-zone climates. It demands frequent, precise mowing (often below half an inch on greens), consistent irrigation, and a disciplined fertility and disease-management program, since its shallow root system and dense canopy are prone to thatch buildup and fungal disease under casual care. Outside of managed turf settings such as golf courses and bowling greens, it is rarely a practical choice for home lawns.
sources: United States Golf Association Green Section

planting.note: Broadcast seed after last frost, once soil has warmed, into moist, acidic, sandy to poorly drained soil in partial shade to full sun; carpetgrass thrives in the low, wet, infertile, acidic soils common across the Gulf Coast where other turf grasses struggle.

directions: Broadcast seed after last frost, once soil has warmed, into moist, acidic, sandy to poorly drained soil in partial shade to full sun; carpetgrass thrives in the low, wet, infertile, acidic soils common across the Gulf Coast where other turf grasses struggle. This coarse-bladed, stoloniferous warm-season grass forms a dense, low-growing sod that tolerates the shade under pines and hardwoods better than bermudagrass or zoysia, and it needs little fertilizer to persist on poor, sandy, wet soils where richer turf grasses fail. It is easy and inexpensive to establish from seed and spreads readily by surface runners, making it a practical, low-input lawn choice for damp, partly shaded Gulf South yards, though it goes dormant and browns at the first hard freeze and is less wear-tolerant than denser turf grasses. Mow regularly through the growing season to prevent seed-stalk formation and keep the sod dense.
